patient.name: Miriam Vanderberg
patient.chief_complaint: Burning pain in feet and hands since age 22, now spreading — multiple physicians have told her 'nothing is wrong'
patient.hpi: Miriam Vanderberg is a 34-year-old graphic designer who has had progressive burning neuropathic pain in her feet since age 22, now involving her hands and lower legs. She has been evaluated by 4 prior physicians including 2 neurologists, all of whom told her standard nerve conduction studies were 'completely normal' and some suggested her symptoms might be anxiety or fibromyalgia. She describes constant burning and aching pain in her feet, worse at night, which prevents her from sleeping. She reports allodynia so severe that bedsheets touching her feet are intolerable. Over the past 3 years, symptoms have extended to her calves and hands. She also reports episodes of episodic facial flushing and sweating disproportionate to ambient temperature, abdominal cramping, constipation alternating with diarrhea, and near-syncope on standing that her internist attributed to dehydration. Her mother had identical symptoms starting in her late 20s and was told she had fibromyalgia before dying at age 59 of 'heart failure of unclear cause.' Her maternal uncle has severe burning foot pain and uses a wheelchair. Her 10-year-old son has intermittent painful episodes in his hands and feet exacerbated by fever. She has no diabetes, no alcohol use, no toxic exposures, and no history of chemotherapy. Multiple metabolic, rheumatological, and infectious workups have been negative at outside institutions. She was diagnosed with 'small fiber neuropathy of unknown etiology' 2 years ago when an outside institution performed skin biopsy, but no further workup was initiated to find the cause. She has trialed gabapentin 1800 mg/day, duloxetine 60 mg, amitriptyline 50 mg, and topical capsaicin with insufficient relief.
pmh: Small fiber neuropathy (diagnosed 2 years ago by outside institution, cause unknown)
Prior diagnoses considered: fibromyalgia, anxiety disorder, functional disorder (all incorrect)
patient.review_of_systems: Positive: burning neuropathic pain feet and hands (since age 22), progressive allodynia, nocturnal pain worse, episodic facial flushing and sweating, orthostatic near-syncope, GI dysmotility (constipation + diarrhea + cramping), heat intolerance, anhidrosis patches on feet and legs (absent sweating). Negative: muscle weakness, joint swelling, rash, dysphagia, diplopia, bowel/bladder incontinence, cognitive impairment.

medications.drug: Gabapentin 600 mg three times daily (partial relief only)

family_history: Mother: burning foot pain from age 28, fibromyalgia label, died at 59 of unexplained cardiac failure. Maternal uncle: severe burning foot pain, wheelchair-bound. Son (age 10): episodic painful crises in hands and feet triggered by fever and exercise. Father: healthy, no neuropathy. AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT INHERITANCE PATTERN — mother, index patient, and son affected across 3 generations.

social_history.note: Graphic designer working from home. Married. Non-smoker. Non-drinker. No illicit drugs. No toxic occupational exposures. Severely limited quality of life from pain — stopped exercise 3 years ago.

results.NCS_interpretation: COMPLETELY NORMAL NCS AND EMG. All sensory amplitudes and velocities normal. All motor amplitudes and velocities normal. No fibrillations on needle EMG. This does NOT exclude neuropathy — standard NCS measures only large myelinated A-alpha (motor) and A-beta (sensory) fibers. Small unmyelinated C-fibers and thinly myelinated A-delta fibers (pain and temperature) are INVISIBLE to standard NCS. Normal NCS in a patient with burning pain and temperature loss confirms SMALL FIBER NEUROPATHY — dedicated SFN testing required.

followup_outputs.interpretation: Normal NCS confirms SFN — standard electrophysiology cannot detect small fiber dysfunction. This matches the outside institution's prior NCS reports. SFN diagnosis requires skin biopsy IENFD or QST.

followup_outputs.indication: Confirm SFN by gold standard intraepidermal nerve fiber density; quantify autonomic small fiber involvement

findings.Skin_biopsy_sites: Right distal leg (10 cm above lateral malleolus) and right proximal thigh
findings.IENFD_distal_leg: 1.4 fibers/mm (SEVERELY REDUCED; normative mean for age/sex 34F = 8.2 ± 2.4 fibers/mm; patient is 3.3 SD below mean)
findings.IENFD_proximal_thigh: 4.8 fibers/mm (REDUCED; normative mean = 16.1 ± 4.2 fibers/mm; patient is 2.7 SD below mean)
findings.IENFD_pattern: LENGTH-DEPENDENT reduction (distal < proximal) consistent with dying-back small fiber axonopathy
findings.Immunostaining: PGP9.5-positive fibers: markedly reduced density. Fiber morphology: beading and fragmentation of surviving fibers (axonal degeneration pattern).
findings.QSART_bilateral_feet: ANHIDROSIS — absent sweat output bilateral feet (0 nL/mm² vs normative >0.5 nL/mm²). Quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test confirms autonomic C-fiber (postganglionic sudomotor) involvement.
findings.QSART_lower_legs: Markedly reduced (0.2 nL/mm² vs normative >1.2 nL/mm²)
findings.QSART_upper_extremities: Mildly reduced bilateral hands (0.4 nL/mm² vs normative >1.0 nL/mm²)

followup_outputs.interpretation: Skin biopsy confirms SEVERE small fiber neuropathy: IENFD 1.4 fibers/mm (3.3 SD below normal). QSART confirms autonomic C-fiber loss. The combination of length-dependent IENFD reduction, QSART anhidrosis, and completely normal NCS/large fiber testing is diagnostic of isolated small fiber neuropathy. Given the severity, 12-year duration, autosomal dominant family history, and multi-system features, hereditary etiology is highly likely. Fabry disease and sodium channelopathy genetic testing are mandatory.

results.Variant_frequency: SCN9A p.Ile739Val — absent from gnomAD (population frequency <1:100,000; not a benign variant)
results.Functional_studies_reference: Previously characterized in Faber et al. 2012 J Neurol: Nav1.7 p.Ile739Val causes constitutive channel activation, DRG neuron hyperexcitability, episodic pain in 3 family members

followup_outputs.interpretation: PATHOGENIC SCN9A (Nav1.7) GAIN-OF-FUNCTION VARIANT IDENTIFIED: c.2215A>G, p.Ile739Val. Nav1.7 is the primary sodium channel in nociceptors (DRG pain neurons) and autonomic neurons. Gain-of-function variants cause constitutive DRG hyperexcitability = hereditary small fiber neuropathy. Autosomal dominant inheritance explains 3-generation family history. Son's episodic pain crises (triggered by fever) = fever-exacerbated Nav1.7 gain-of-function (channel opens at lower temperature threshold). Mother's death from cardiac failure: SCN9A variants can rarely involve cardiac Nav1.7 — cardiac evaluation warranted. Fabry disease excluded (normal Gb3, no GLA mutation).

followup_outputs.query: SCN9A Nav1.7 gain-of-function hereditary small fiber neuropathy treatment sodium channel

results.title: Gain-of-function Nav1.7 mutations as a continuum: A1632E displays physiological changes associated with erythromelalgia and paroxysmal extreme pain disorder
results.key_finding: Nav1.7 gain-of-function mutations cause a spectrum from erythromelalgia (severe episodic burning) to paroxysmal extreme pain disorder to small fiber neuropathy. Mutations cause constitutive DRG sodium channel opening, lowering action potential threshold. Temperature sensitivity explains fever-triggered episodes.

results.title: Sodium channelopathies in small fiber neuropathy: prevalence and treatment with lacosamide
results.key_finding: SCN9A/SCN10A/SCN11A pathogenic variants found in 28% of patients with idiopathic SFN who undergo genetic testing. Lacosamide (slow sodium channel inactivator) reduces Nav1.7 gain-of-function and provides superior pain relief vs standard treatments in SCN9A-positive patients. Carbamazepine and mexiletine have been used with variable success. Standard gabapentin/pregabalin less effective for channelopathy-SFN vs inflammatory SFN.

results.title: Hereditary small fiber neuropathy: clinical phenotype and genetic landscape
results.key_finding: Hereditary SFN presents in 2nd-3rd decade, multi-system features (autonomic, possibly cardiac), autosomal dominant SCN9A/SCN10A/SCN11A variants. Children may present with episodic pain. Genetic testing recommended in all SFN patients under age 40 with family history. IVIG and immunosuppression ineffective (not inflammatory). Genetic counseling for affected families.

interactions.description: Both have CYP2C19 involvement at high doses but no clinically significant interaction at standard doses. Monitor for additive CNS effects (dizziness). No dose adjustment required.

Carbamazepine is a strong CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 inducer — significantly reduces duloxetine plasma levels (30-50% reduction). If carbamazepine is used, duloxetine dose adjustment or replacement required. Consider lacosamide instead (no enzyme induction).
No pharmacokinetic interaction. Complementary mechanisms (gabapentin: alpha-2-delta calcium channel; lacosamide: sodium channel slow inactivation). Combination may be used together.

followup_outputs.contraindications: No absolute contraindications to lacosamide. QTc monitoring recommended with lacosamide (can prolong QTc slightly — obtain baseline ECG). Carbamazepine preferred only if lacosamide fails and duloxetine is discontinued.
followup_outputs.recommendations: Trial lacosamide 100 mg twice daily, titrating to 200 mg twice daily over 4 weeks. This is the sodium channel-directed therapy most supported by evidence for Nav1.7 gain-of-function SFN. Continue gabapentin and duloxetine during lacosamide titration. Son should be evaluated by pediatric neurology for genetic testing — if positive, proactive management before severe fiber loss. Genetic counseling for all first-degree relatives.

findings.Thermoregulatory_sweat_test: Anhidrosis bilateral feet and calves (50% body surface area anhidrosis — significant autonomic C-fiber loss)
findings.QSART_confirmation: Confirms postganglionic sudomotor fiber loss — consistent with SFN

followup_outputs.interpretation: Autonomic battery confirms small fiber autonomic neuropathy: orthostatic hypotension (30 mmHg systolic drop), reduced Valsalva ratio (sympathetic failure), anhidrosis 50% BSA, blunted NE rise on standing. Management: increased fluid and salt intake, compression stockings, midodrine 5 mg TID (if persistent orthostatic symptoms), fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. Avoid dehydration.

Exclude Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A, lyso-Gb3, GLA sequencing) — treatable hereditary SFN mimic
Confirm SFN with skin biopsy IENFD and QSART — NCS is always normal in SFN (normal NCS does NOT exclude SFN)
Trial lacosamide for Nav1.7 gain-of-function (sodium channel-directed therapy superior to standard agents)
Genetic counseling for first-degree relatives — autosomal dominant, son at 50% risk and already symptomatic
Refer son to pediatric neurology for genetic testing and early monitoring
Cardiac MRI to evaluate for fibrosis given mother's unexplained cardiac death — annual monitoring

pitfalls: Trusting normal NCS to exclude neuropathy — NCS is NORMAL in small fiber neuropathy by definition (large fibers are intact)
Diagnosing fibromyalgia or anxiety when burning pain + normal NCS is present — should prompt skin biopsy for IENFD
Stopping workup after confirming 'SFN of unknown etiology' — hereditary causes must be actively sought, especially in young patients
Not ordering SCN9A/SCN10A/SCN11A gene panel in early-onset SFN with family history
Missing Fabry disease workup (GLA, lyso-Gb3) — most common treatable hereditary SFN cause
Using carbamazepine without checking duloxetine interaction (CYP induction significantly reduces duloxetine levels)
Not evaluating son — positive family history + episodic pain in a child requires proactive genetic evaluation
Ignoring mother's cardiac death — sodium channelopathies may have cardiac phenotype requiring monitoring

teaching_points: Normal NCS does NOT exclude neuropathy — standard NCS is blind to small C-fibers and A-delta fibers; SFN diagnosis requires skin biopsy IENFD or QST
Skin biopsy IENFD is the gold standard for SFN diagnosis — severely reduced fibers/mm confirms neuropathy when NCS is normal
Genetic testing for SCN9A/SCN10A/SCN11A should be performed in all SFN patients under 40, especially with family history — 28% prevalence in young-onset idiopathic SFN
Nav1.7 gain-of-function causes constitutive DRG hyperexcitability — lacosamide (slow sodium channel inactivator) is superior to gabapentin/pregabalin for this mechanism
Always exclude Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A, lyso-Gb3, GLA sequencing) in young SFN patients — treatable enzyme replacement therapy available
Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern (3 generations) + early onset (age 22) + multisystem autonomic features = hereditary SFN until proven otherwise
Son's episodic pain crises triggered by fever are pathognomonic for Nav1.7 temperature-sensitive gain-of-function — proactive genetic counseling
Fibromyalgia diagnosis in young patients with burning pain should always prompt SFN evaluation (skin biopsy) — SFN is a common underlying cause of fibromyalgia phenotype
